meta.title: Cantonese B1 Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1000 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Cantonese → English (see the Cantonese, recall the meaning) and English → Cantonese (see an English meaning, recall the Cantonese). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1000 words for an intermediate learner, aligned to B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.' — a learner here is able to deal with most situations likely to arise while travelling, to produce simple connected text on familiar topics, and to describe experiences and events, dreams, hopes and ambitions, and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. THIS IS SPOKEN HONG KONG CANTONESE, the language people talk in, not the written Chinese Hong Kong reads and writes, which is close to Mandarin: 佢 for he or she, 喺 for at, 嘢 for a thing, 睇 to look, and the sentence-final particles that carry a Cantonese speaker's tone of voice. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no examination publishes a graded word list for Cantonese, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 395 of the 1000 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — work and careers, money, banking and the economy, education, the news, media and technology, government, law and society, the environment, health and medicine, travel, transport and accommodation, the household and its chores, relationships and the stages of life, feelings and character, Hong Kong customs and beliefs, the nouns for ideas, reasons and plans, the words that join sentences, and the verbs of thinking, deciding, arguing and changing — and the other 605 are the commonest remaining words of spoken Cantonese, counted in the Hong Kong Cantonese Corpus (recorded conversations and radio, 1997–98). The cards are dealt by how often the words are heard there and in Tatoeba's Cantonese sentences, so the commonest come first. Every headword is printed in the traditional characters Hong Kong uses, with the simplified form beneath where it differs, and in Jyutping, the Linguistic Society of Hong Kong's romanisation, which ends every syllable with its TONE as a digit: 1 high, 2 high rising, 3 mid, 4 low falling, 5 low rising, 6 low — because a Cantonese syllable said on the wrong tone is a different word (si1 poem, si4 time, si6 yes). The Cantonese Jyutping and Tones deck, the first in this collection, teaches the sounds and the six tones. The part of speech is the one the corpus's annotators gave the word, and the classifiers a noun is counted with are taught as words of their own rather than printed on the noun. Example sentences come with 248 of the 1000 words, three apiece for 49 of them — Tatoeba's Cantonese is small, so many words have none — with the word picked out in colour, a speaker beside each sentence, and the Jyutping beneath it where every word in the sentence carries a reading the dictionaries confirm. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings: CC-CEDICT (MDBG, CC BY-SA 4.0) and CC-Canto (Pleco, CC BY-SA 3.0). Jyutping: CC-Canto and its Cantonese readings of CC-CEDICT (Pleco, CC BY-SA 3.0), and the Hong Kong Cantonese Corpus. Frequency and parts of speech: the Hong Kong Cantonese Corpus, HKCanCor (Luke Kang Kwong; CC BY 4.0, as distributed with PyCantonese), and Tatoeba. Example sentences and their Jyutping: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
